title: Halo Effect
description: One positive trait unconsciously makes you assume they have many other positive traits—intelligence, kindness, competence.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: One positive trait (attractiveness, confidence, a prestigious alma mater) unconsciously makes you assume they have many other positive traits—intelligence, kindness, competence.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A well-dressed candidate is rated as more capable before speaking.
A charismatic speaker says something mediocre but gets applause; the same words from a dull speaker would be ignored.
You automatically trust a doctor more because their office is clean and they wear a white coat, even before they demonstrate medical skill.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Interviewers making up their mind in the first 10 seconds based on appearance and demeanor.
People paying more for products with beautiful packaging, assuming quality.
Overlooking flaws in attractive or confident individuals.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re impressed by someone’s confidence and instantly assume they’re right.
You dismiss contrary data because “they seem so competent.”
You assume good-looking people are more honest (physical attractiveness stereotype).

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Brains conserve energy by using shortcuts. A strong positive signal becomes a central trait that colors everything else.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Separate domains: Ask “Is this person’s appearance relevant to their advice?”
Objectively sample performance data, not just impressions.
When you notice strong positive or negative feelings toward someone, list their traits independently, as if rating a stranger.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Believing you’re not susceptible because you’re a critical thinker. Halo effects are largely unconscious.
Rejecting a candidate entirely due to one negative trait (reverse halo / devil effect).

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: Two consultants pitch the same idea. One is impeccably dressed, speaks with a British accent, and uses elegant slides. The other, in casual clothes, presents the same data nervously. The board approves the first without scrutinizing the second’s equally solid proposal.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Likeability is a tinted lens. Before deciding, wipe the lens clean and look at the evidence in black and white.
